name: Breast cancer
summary: Cancer that forms in the cells of the breast, most often in the ducts or lobules. It is one of the most common cancers worldwide and is classified by hormone-receptor (ER/PR) and HER2 status, which guide treatment.
symptoms: New lump in the breast or underarm
Change in breast size or shape
screening: The US Preventive Services Task Force (2024) recommends a mammogram every 2 years for women ages 40 to 74. Some groups, such as the American Cancer Society, advise yearly mammograms at some ages, and women at higher risk may need to start earlier or have extra imaging. Talk with a clinician about what's right for you.

name: Lung cancer
summary: Cancer that forms in the tissues of the lung. The two main types are non-small cell lung cancer (about 85%) and small cell lung cancer. It is a leading cause of cancer death worldwide; biomarker testing (EGFR, ALK, KRAS, PD-L1 and others) guides treatment.
screening: The US Preventive Services Task Force (2021) recommends a yearly low-dose CT scan for adults 50 to 80 who have a 20 pack-year smoking history and smoke now or quit within the past 15 years. The American Cancer Society (2023) no longer limits screening by years since quitting. Ask a clinician whether you qualify.

name: Prostate cancer
summary: Cancer that forms in the prostate gland. Many prostate cancers grow slowly; options range from active surveillance to surgery, radiation and hormone-based therapies.
screening: The US Preventive Services Task Force (2018) says men 55 to 69 should decide with a clinician whether to have a PSA blood test, and recommends against PSA screening at 70 and older. The American Urological Association suggests a first (baseline) PSA test at 45 to 50, or earlier for men at higher risk.

name: Colorectal cancer
summary: Cancer of the colon or rectum, usually developing from polyps over many years. Screening can find and remove polyps before they become cancer.
screening: The US Preventive Services Task Force (2021) recommends screening for adults 45 to 75. Colonoscopy and stool tests (FIT or stool DNA) are the standard options. FDA-approved blood tests (such as Shield, approved in 2024) find many cancers but miss most precancerous polyps, so they are mainly for people who decline colonoscopy and stool tests. A positive result on any test other than colonoscopy needs a follow-up colonoscopy.

name: Skin cancer (melanoma)
summary: Melanoma begins in pigment-producing cells (melanocytes) and is the most serious common skin cancer. Basal and squamous cell skin cancers are more common and usually less aggressive.
symptoms: Diameter larger than a pencil eraser
screening: The US Preventive Services Task Force (2023) found not enough evidence to recommend for or against routine skin exams by a clinician for adults without symptoms. Check your own skin and see a clinician about any new, changing or unusual spot or mole.

name: Leukemia
summary: Cancers of blood-forming tissue that produce abnormal white blood cells. Main types are acute myeloid (AML), acute lymphoblastic (ALL), chronic myeloid (CML) and chronic lymphocytic (CLL) leukemia.
symptoms: Swollen lymph nodes or enlarged spleen
screening: No routine screening; often found through blood tests.

name: Lymphoma
summary: Cancers that begin in lymphocytes of the immune system. They are grouped into Hodgkin lymphoma and many subtypes of non-Hodgkin lymphoma, such as diffuse large B-cell and follicular lymphoma.
screening: No routine screening.

name: Pancreatic cancer
summary: Cancer that forms in the pancreas, most commonly pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. It is often diagnosed at an advanced stage.
screening: No routine screening for average-risk people; surveillance may be offered to some high-risk individuals.
treatments: Targeted therapy for specific gene changes

name: Cervical cancer
summary: Cancer of the cervix, almost always caused by long-lasting infection with high-risk types of human papillomavirus (HPV). It is largely preventable through vaccination and screening.
screening: Ages 21–29: a Pap test every 3 years. Ages 30–65: an HPV test every 5 years, a Pap test every 3 years, or both tests every 5 years. Updated US women's preventive services guidelines (HRSA, 2026) prefer the HPV test, and the American Cancer Society recommends it every 5 years from age 25. The FDA now allows HPV testing on a sample you collect yourself, in a clinic (since 2024) or with an at-home kit (since 2025). HPV vaccination prevents most cases.
